mcqs.question: What is a Java applet?

options.B: A small Java program embedded in a web page for interactive content

mcqs.explanation: An applet is a small Java program designed to be embedded in web pages. It runs inside a web browser (or appletviewer) and provides interactive GUI content — buttons, text fields, animations — making web pages dynamic.

mcqs.question: What does an applet window contain?

options.B: A title bar, status area, and a display/view area

mcqs.explanation: An applet window has: a title bar at the top, a status area at the bottom (showStatus()), and the main display/view area where graphics and GUI components are rendered. This mirrors standard window structure.

mcqs.question: Which package provides the Applet class?

options.B: java.applet

mcqs.explanation: java.applet contains the Applet class. To write an applet: import java.applet.Applet; then extend Applet: public class MyApplet extends Applet { ... }. The Graphics class for drawing comes from java.awt.

mcqs.question: What is the applet lifecycle order?

options.B: init → start → paint → stop → destroy

mcqs.explanation: Applet lifecycle: init() (called once on load) → start() (called after init, and each time page is revisited) → paint() (draws content) → stop() (when leaving page) → destroy() (when applet is unloaded).

mcqs.question: Which applet method is called exactly once when the applet is first loaded?

options.B: paint()

mcqs.explanation: init() is called exactly once when the applet is first loaded. It's used for one-time initialization: creating components, setting colors, loading images, setting layout. After init(), start() is called.

mcqs.question: Which applet method is called each time the user returns to the page containing the applet?

options.B: start()

mcqs.explanation: start() is called after init() and each time the user revisits the page. It resumes applet execution (e.g., restarting animations, resuming threads). stop() is called when leaving the page — the pair manages pause/resume.

mcqs.question: What does repaint() do in an applet?

options.B: Triggers a redraw by calling update() which calls paint()

mcqs.explanation: repaint() schedules a redraw. It calls update() which clears the area and calls paint(). Use repaint() when you need to refresh the display (e.g., after changing data that paint() displays). It's asynchronous — returns immediately.

mcqs.question: Which method displays a message in the applet's status bar?

options.B: showStatus("message")

mcqs.explanation: showStatus(String msg) displays text in the browser/appletviewer status bar at the bottom. Example: showStatus("Loading..."). Useful for user feedback without adding text to the applet's display area.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of the paint() method in an applet?

options.B: To draw graphics and text on the applet's display area

mcqs.explanation: paint(Graphics g) draws the applet's visual content: text (drawString), shapes (drawRect, drawOval, drawLine), and images (drawImage). The Graphics object 'g' is the 'brush'. paint() is called by the system whenever the applet needs redrawing.

mcqs.question: How do you get the width and height of an applet?

options.B: getWidth() and getHeight() methods

mcqs.explanation: getWidth() returns the applet's width in pixels (as set by the HTML width attribute). getHeight() returns height. Used for positioning elements relative to applet size: g.drawString("Hi", getWidth()/2, getHeight()/2) centers text.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between init() and start() in the applet lifecycle?

options.B: init() is called once on load for setup; start() is called after init AND each time the page is revisited to resume execution
options.D: init() handles graphics; start() handles events

mcqs.explanation: init() runs once when the applet first loads — perfect for one-time setup (create components, set layout). start() runs after init() and each time the user returns to the page — use it to resume threads, animations, or timers. stop() pauses when leaving.

mcqs.question: How does an applet differ from a regular Java application?

options.B: Applets don't have main() — they use init(), start(), paint() lifecycle; run in browser/appletviewer with security restrictions
options.D: Applets can access local files freely

mcqs.explanation: Applications have main() and run via 'java' command with full system access. Applets have init/start/paint lifecycle, run in browsers/appletviewer, and have security restrictions (sandbox): can't read local files, can't execute programs, can only connect to the originating server.

mcqs.question: What are applet security restrictions (sandbox)?

options.B: Cannot read/write local files, cannot start programs, cannot connect to servers other than the one it was loaded from

mcqs.explanation: Applets run in a security sandbox to prevent malicious code from harming the user's system. Restrictions: no local file access, no executing programs, no loading native libraries, network connections only to the originating host. Signed applets can request expanded permissions.

mcqs.question: How do you pass parameters from HTML to an applet?

options.B: Using <param name="x" value="y"> inside the <applet> tag, then getParameter("x") in Java

mcqs.explanation: HTML: <applet code='App.class' width=300 height=300><param name='color' value='red'></applet>. Java: String color = getParameter("color"); — returns "red". Parameters are always strings; convert with Integer.parseInt() etc. Allows customizing applet behavior without recompiling.

mcqs.question: What does getParameter() return if the parameter is not specified in the HTML?

options.B: Returns null

mcqs.explanation: getParameter("name") returns null if the parameter is not defined in the HTML. Always check: String val = getParameter("speed"); if(val != null) speed = Integer.parseInt(val); else speed = DEFAULT_SPEED;

mcqs.question: What is getCodeBase() used for in an applet?

options.A: Returns the source code of the applet
options.B: Returns the URL of the directory from which the applet class file was loaded

mcqs.explanation: getCodeBase() returns the URL of the applet's code directory. If the applet is at http://example.com/applets/MyApplet.class, getCodeBase() returns http://example.com/applets/. Used with getImage(getCodeBase(), "logo.png") to load resources relative to the applet's location.

mcqs.question: What is getDocumentBase() and how does it differ from getCodeBase()?

options.B: getDocumentBase() returns the URL of the HTML page containing the applet; getCodeBase() returns the URL of the applet's .class file directory

mcqs.explanation: getDocumentBase(): URL of the HTML page that embeds the applet (e.g., http://example.com/index.html). getCodeBase(): URL of the applet's .class files (e.g., http://example.com/applets/). They may differ if the HTML is in a different directory than the class files.

mcqs.question: How do you set the background color of an applet?

options.B: applet.background = yellow

mcqs.explanation: setBackground(Color.YELLOW) sets the applet's background. Call in init() for one-time setup. Colors: Color.RED, Color.BLUE, Color.GREEN, or custom: new Color(255, 200, 0). The foreground (text color) is set with setForeground().

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of update() in the applet paint cycle?

options.B: Clears the applet area with the background color, then calls paint() — part of the repaint() cycle

mcqs.explanation: repaint() → update() → paint(). update() clears the drawing area by filling with the background color, then calls paint(). This causes flicker for animations. To reduce flicker: override update() to not clear (just call paint()), or use double buffering.

mcqs.question: Which method is used to draw a rectangle in an applet?

options.B: g.rectangle(x, y, w, h)

mcqs.explanation: g.drawRect(x, y, width, height) draws a rectangle outline with top-left at (x,y). g.fillRect(x, y, w, h) draws a filled rectangle. Coordinates are in pixels with (0,0) at the top-left corner of the applet.

mcqs.question: Why does a simple animation in an applet flicker, and what are the solutions?

options.B: update() clears the entire area before paint() — each clear+redraw causes flicker. Solutions: override update() to skip clearing, use double buffering (BufferStrategy), or use Swing's auto double-buffered JPanel
options.C: Flicker is caused by network latency

mcqs.explanation: Flickering happens because update() fills the background then paint() draws — between these two operations, the screen briefly shows the cleared state. Solutions: 1) Override update() to call paint() directly without clearing, 2) Double buffering — draw to an off-screen image first, then copy to screen in one operation, 3) Swing components (JApplet, JPanel) have built-in double buffering.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between Applet and JApplet?

options.B: JApplet (javax.swing) extends Applet, adds Swing features: built-in double buffering, content pane, better look-and-feel, lightweight components

mcqs.explanation: JApplet (javax.swing.JApplet) extends java.applet.Applet. It adds: content pane (add components via getContentPane().add()), built-in double buffering (no flicker), Swing lightweight components (JButton, JTextField), pluggable look-and-feel. Modern applet development uses JApplet, though applets themselves are deprecated in modern browsers.

mcqs.question: What is the 'applet sandbox' security model and why was it necessary?

options.A: It's a GUI sandbox for drawing
options.B: It restricts applet actions to prevent malicious web-loaded code from accessing the user's system — no file access, no native code, network only to origin server

mcqs.explanation: Applets are downloaded from web servers and run on the user's machine — potentially untrusted code. The sandbox restricts them: no local file I/O, no executing programs, no native libraries, no System.exit(), network connections only to the originating host. Signed applets can request all-permissions to escape the sandbox, but the user must trust the signature.

mcqs.question: Why are Java applets largely obsolete in modern web development, and what replaced them?

options.B: Browsers removed Java plugin support due to security risks; HTML5 (Canvas, WebGL, WebSockets), JavaScript frameworks (React, Vue), and WebAssembly replaced applets' use cases

mcqs.explanation: Modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) removed NPAPI/Java plugin support around 2015-2017 due to repeated security vulnerabilities. HTML5 Canvas/WebGL provide graphics, WebSockets provide networking, JavaScript provides interactivity — all without plugins. Java applets are now legacy technology. The NPTEL course predates this shift.

mcqs.question: How does double buffering eliminate flickering in applet animations?

options.B: Draw everything to an off-screen Image buffer first, then copy the complete buffer to the screen in one operation — the screen never shows a partially drawn frame

mcqs.explanation: Without double buffering: update() clears screen → flicker → paint() draws. With double buffering: create an off-screen Image, draw everything to it (g.drawImage, g.drawString), then in paint() copy the off-screen image to the visible graphics context in one drawImage() call. The screen always shows a complete frame — no flicker. Swing components do this automatically.

mcqs.question: What is MediaTracker and why is it needed when loading images in applets?

options.B: MediaTracker synchronizes image loading — it ensures images are fully loaded before they're drawn, preventing partial/blank images

mcqs.explanation: getImage() is asynchronous — it returns immediately but the image may still be downloading. Drawing an unloaded image shows nothing. MediaTracker tracks loading: tracker.addImage(img, 0); tracker.waitForID(0); blocks until image 0 is fully loaded. Then drawImage() displays correctly. Modern alternative: ImageIO.read() which is synchronous.

mcqs.question: In an applet, what happens if stop() is not properly implemented in an animation applet?

options.A: No issue — the browser handles it
options.B: The animation thread keeps running in the background even when the user leaves the page, wasting CPU and potentially causing errors when the applet is destroyed

mcqs.explanation: If start() creates a thread for animation but stop() doesn't suspend/stop it, the thread keeps running after the user navigates away. This wastes CPU, may try to draw to a non-visible component, and causes issues when destroy() is called. Proper pattern: stop() should set a flag (running=false) or call thread.suspend() (deprecated) so the thread exits cleanly.

mcqs.question: How can an applet communicate with JavaScript in the browser?

options.B: Using netscape.javascript.JSObject: JSObject.getWindow(applet).eval("alert('Hi')") — allows calling JavaScript from Java and vice versa with MAYSCRIPT attribute

mcqs.explanation: JSObject (from netscape.javascript package, available in browsers with Java plugin) enables bidirectional communication: Java applet calls JavaScript (js.eval, js.call, js.getMember), JavaScript calls Java (document.appletName.methodName()). Requires MAYSCRIPT attribute in the <applet> tag. This bridged Java's power with the browser's DOM.

mcqs.question: What is the significance of the ARCHIVE attribute in the <applet> HTML tag?

options.B: Specifies a JAR file containing the applet classes — reduces HTTP requests by downloading one compressed archive instead of multiple .class files

mcqs.explanation: <applet code='MyApplet.class' archive='applet.jar' ...> tells the browser to download applet.jar (containing all class files and resources) in one request instead of downloading each .class separately. This dramatically reduces load time for applets with many classes — one compressed download vs many uncompressed ones.

mcqs.question: What is the fundamental architectural difference between an applet's event handling (delegation event model) and a traditional procedural event loop?

options.B: Procedural: single loop polls for events (blocking, sequential). Applet/Java AWT: delegation model — components register listeners; events are dispatched asynchronously to specific listener methods (event-driven, non-blocking)

mcqs.explanation: Traditional event loop: while(true) { event = waitForEvent(); handle(event); } — blocks, handles one event at a time, tightly coupled. Java's delegation event model: components (buttons, text fields) maintain listener lists; when an event occurs, the event dispatch thread calls each registered listener's handler method (actionPerformed, mouseClicked, etc.). This is modular, decoupled, and supports multiple independent listeners per component.
